summary: For 5-6 year olds, sorting into categories is an early step of the statistical process, after posing a question: choose one attribute, classify every object into non-overlapping groups, count each group, and order groups by count to find most/fewest. Make the sorting RULE explicit and fixed (one attribute at a time), physically arrange groups so counts can be compared fairly, and anchor to a real question ('which colour do we have most of?'). Work with real objects the child handles so counts are concrete before any chart appears.
misconceptions: Shifts the sorting criterion partway (starts by colour, drifts to size), producing mixed groups
Judges 'most' by the space a group takes up rather than its count (a spread-out group of big objects looks like 'more')
Miscounts a group by losing track when objects are scattered (insecure cardinality)
Thinks each object can go in more than one pile, or leaves objects unsorted

activities.title: Drag-to-sort (or hands-on sort) with self-counting groups
steps: Face a jumble of coloured shapes and three labelled groups/bins (physical trays or an on-screen mat).
Before starting, say aloud the single attribute: 'we are sorting by COLOUR.'
Move each shape into its matching group until every shape is placed and none is left over.

Watch or build each group as a line with one object per equal-sized space (or a stack of same-size counters standing for the objects) so groups can be compared fairly, and keep a running count of each group.
Read off which group has the most and which has the fewest by comparing the counts.
Then re-sort the SAME set a different way (by size): tip everything out, relabel the groups, and sort again, noticing the counts change.
activities.insight: Sorting means applying one consistent rule to classify every object, and 'most/fewest' is read from the counts once the groups are arranged for fair comparison. The same fixed data can also be grouped in more than one way — how you sort is a choice.

activities.title: Sort the same set two different ways
steps: Take one set of objects and sort it by colour; count and record each group (category name + count).
Tip the set out and sort the SAME objects by a second attribute (size: big/small); count and record again.
Compare the two records and talk about how the groups and their counts differ even though the objects are identical.
activities.insight: The data is fixed, but the grouping is a choice; different attributes give different groups and different counts.

activities.title: Answer a real question from sorted class data
steps: Pose a real question first, e.g. 'which colour do we have most of?' or use data the child helped generate (favourite colour, shape cards).
Sort and count to answer it, then read the result back against the question: 'so we have most red — does that answer our question?'
State both the most and the fewest category by their counts (or say that groups tie when their counts are equal).
activities.insight: Sorting and counting are done for a purpose — to answer a question about real data — not as an isolated exercise.

checkQuestion: Here is a mixed pile of coloured counters. Sort them so we can see how many of each colour there are, then tell me which colour we have the most of and which the fewest. (Set the task, then WATCH — do not tell them how to sort.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: the child picks one attribute (colour) and sorts EVERY counter into non-overlapping groups, counts each group accurately (last-number-said = how many), and names the largest and smallest groups by their counts — ideally lining the groups up to compare.
